sections.title: Error Spotting Level 2 Strategy
sections.content: In Level 2, errors are slightly more subtle. Solve in 3-4 steps: Step 1: Understand the sentence structure. Step 2: Identify the Clause or Phrase. Step 3: Apply grammar rules (Conditionals, Parallelism, etc.). Step 4: Check if the meaning is logical.

sections.title: Errors in Conditional Sentences
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the If-clause. Step 2: Check which type it is (Zero, First, Second, Third). Step 3: 'will' is generally not used in the If-clause (in the First conditional). Step 4: Use the correct tense in the Main clause. Example: 'If I will go there, I will meet him' is wrong. Correct: 'If I go there, I will meet him.'

sections.title: Parallelism / Parallel Structure
sections.content: Step 1: Identify a list or conjunction (and, or). Step 2: Check the form of all items (verb-ing, noun, infinitive). Step 3: Keep all of them in the same form. Step 4: Check for structural balance. Example: 'He likes dancing, swimming, and to read' is wrong. Correct: 'He likes dancing, swimming, and reading.'

sections.title: Dangling or Misplaced Modifiers
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the Modifier (-ing phrase). Step 2: See which subject it is modifying. Step 3: Ensure that the correct subject immediately follows the modifier. Step 4: Check if the meaning is clear. Example: 'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful' is wrong because trees cannot walk. Correct: 'Walking down the street, I saw beautiful trees.'

sections.title: Correlative Conjunction Errors
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the pair (Not only... but also, Either... or, Neither... nor). Step 2: Keep the grammatical form identical in both parts. Step 3: Make the verb agree with the nearest subject (for Either/Neither). Step 4: Check the balance. Example: 'Not only he sings but also dances' is wrong. Correct: 'He not only sings but also dances.'

sections.title: Phrasal Verbs and Fixed Prepositions
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the Verb. Step 2: Check which preposition is fixed to it. Step 3: Ensure the meaning isn't changing incorrectly. Step 4: Match it with standard usage. Example: 'He is good in maths' is wrong. Correct: 'He is good at maths.'

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using 'will' in the If-clause. 2. Mixing different forms in a list. 3. Attaching a modifier to the wrong subject. 4. Creating an imbalance in correlative conjunctions. 5. Using the wrong preposition.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 2, focus on both structure and meaning. Remember the tense rules in Conditionals, maintain identical forms in Parallelism, attach the correct subject to Modifiers, and use Fixed prepositions correctly.

tricks.title: If + Present Rule
tricks.explanation: In the First conditional, the If-clause takes the present tense, and the main clause takes 'will'.
tricks.example: If she studies, she will pass.

tricks.title: List Same Form Rule
tricks.explanation: Keep all words after And/Or in the exact same form.
tricks.example: She likes reading, writing, and painting.

tricks.title: Check Subject After Modifier
tricks.explanation: The -ing phrase must be immediately followed by the subject actually performing that action.
tricks.example: Driving home, he saw an accident.

tricks.title: Not Only Placement
tricks.explanation: Place 'Not only' before the verb and keep the structure perfectly balanced.
tricks.example: She not only sings but also dances.

tricks.title: Either/Neither Verb Rule
tricks.explanation: The verb will always agree with the nearest subject.
tricks.example: Either Ram or his friends are coming.

tricks.title: Remember Fixed Prepositions
tricks.explanation: Certain verbs and adjectives take specific, fixed prepositions.
tricks.example: Interested in, Afraid of, Good at.

tricks.title: Second Conditional Identification
tricks.explanation: Look for the structure: If + past tense, would + base verb.
tricks.example: If I were rich, I would travel.

tricks.title: Meaning Check Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Read the sentence logically to see if the subject makes sense in context.
tricks.example: Running fast, the car crashed. (Incorrect subject reference)
